claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a supersaturated, homogeneous FCC microstructure.
The as-built alloy contains minimal pre-existing oxide precipitates or voids.
Gas-environment-induced microstructural instabilities govern degradation and catastrophic failure during exposure at 900–1000 K.
Under oxidizing conditions, selective oxidation of Al and Ti produces nanoscale Al2O3 and TiO2 precipitates.
Oxide precipitates generate localized residual-stress fields and elastic undulations in the FCC matrix.
The proposed oxide-associated nanoscale undulations are analogous to elastic undulations associated with deformation twinning.
Oxidation-induced elastic undulations localize strain and initiate microcracks.
Under reducing conditions, failure to form a protective oxide scale enhances vacancy diffusion and vacancy accumulation.
Vacancies nucleate and coalesce into voids preferentially along grain boundaries under reducing conditions.
Grain-boundary voids promote localized dislocation-slip-band propagation and catastrophic failure.
Oxidizing exposure will cause a measurable loss of ductility and fracture toughness relative to the as-built state.
Reducing exposure will produce minimal oxide formation but increased grain-boundary-void density and slip-band activity.
Failure after reducing exposure will be more abrupt and catastrophic than the degradation observed in the oxidizing environment.
The as-built alloy has high ductility and toughness before elevated-temperature exposure.
The proposed behavior applies from 900–1000 K for exposures of 100–300 hours under the specified oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
Departures from the stated temperature, duration, or atmosphere may produce alternative degradation pathways.
High-resolution in-situ or synchrotron-based characterization is necessary to establish a conclusive correlation between nanoscale elastic undulations and microcrack nucleation.
